Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Leila was nineteen when her two-year-old son, Amir, woke from a nap with a fever so high that his small body trembled. She drove him to the emergency room in the middle of the night, her boyfriend, Tariq, silent in the passenger seat. By morning, doctors told them it was bacterial meningitis. Leila remembers the exact sound of the word—how it slid out of the physician’s mouth and landed in her chest like a stone. She spent the next ten days in a pediatric intensive care unit, watching numbers on monitors, holding Amir’s hand through the rails of a crib bed. When he finally recovered, everyone told her she had done everything right. But Leila could not stop replaying the hours before the fever. She had thought it was just a cold. She had given him Tylenol and put him down for a nap. That delay—those hours—felt like a failure she could never undo.

In the months after, Leila returned to her warehouse job, but her mind no longer cooperated. She stood at a packing station, scanning barcodes and sealing boxes, and found herself unable to hold a thought for more than a few seconds. Instructions from her supervisor slipped away the moment they were spoken. She would reach for a roll of tape and then freeze, unable to remember what she had been about to do. The warehouse's constant hum—conveyor belts, rolling carts, the beep of scanners—seemed to press into her skull, making it impossible to focus. More than once she had to re-count an entire pallet because she lost track halfway through.

Small, ordinary moments triggered something she could not control. A child coughing in the grocery store made her heart lurch and her palms go slick. The sound of a siren, even blocks away, sent heat rushing up her neck and a tightness across her chest so sudden she had to brace herself against a wall. Each time, a wave of fear would hit, then horror at the memory of Amir limp and gray on the hospital bed, followed by a sharp spike of anger at herself—for not noticing sooner, for being so stupid—and then a thick blanket of shame. She had come to believe that these reactions proved she was a weak person. Other mothers, she was certain, would have handled the crisis with calm strength. They would not still be jumping at every cough months later. She told herself repeatedly that she should have protected Amir from ever becoming that ill, and she had failed. No one else blamed her, but Leila’s own mind had become a relentless prosecutor.

Tariq tried to reassure her, but his words only deepened her guilt. She could not shake the belief that bad things were always waiting to happen, and that she was powerless to stop them. At work, she began to dread certain aisles of the warehouse—the one near the breakroom where someone had once left a half-empty bottle of children’s acetaminophen on a shelf. She did not avoid it deliberately; she simply found herself taking longer routes without thinking. But avoidance was not the problem she named when she finally scheduled an appointment at a community mental health clinic. What she told the intake worker was that she could not concentrate well enough to keep her job, and that her boyfriend had started to say she seemed distant and angry for no reason. She was afraid, she said, that she would never feel like a capable mother again, and that this sense of helplessness would follow her forever. She wanted the physical jolt to stop whenever she saw a thermometer. She wanted to stop feeling like a fraud when someone told her she was strong. Mostly, she wanted to believe that she might, eventually, be able to keep something bad from happening.
